_note: E3 helpdesk-vishing attack fragment (P7-Q). A fragment of the `social` block; the full-episode shell (P7-Y2) copies these keys into scenarios/awareness_e3_*/scenario.json.erb and the defend-only/check shells (P7-Y1) leave the attack out. All companies and people are fictional (BRAND_SET.md, Quayholt Insurance). The learner, a junior red-teamer on an authorised Quayholt exercise, impersonates Gordon McLeish, a locked-out Claims Manager, and phones the IT service desk (character `leila` = Leila Nassar) to talk her into a password reset. No reset code, number or real procedure is shown; the NPC's policy is a deliberately weak one, so the lesson is that its two 'security' answers are both findable online. The second attack beat is the MFA-fatigue decision (see `mfaDecision`): having 'reset' Gordon in the call, the learner now chooses when to fire approval prompts and how many, then watches the worn-down target tap approve. Every combination lands (no dead end), and the authenticator overlay's outcome panel explains which conditions made it work and names the defender's control. Was a watch-only demo (`pushStream`); turned into a learner decision per FUN_DECISIONS q_e3mfa (2026-10-27) / P5 finding E3-11. See the P7-Q report for the globals the shell must declare, the `knows` id list P7-S draws from, and the attack->defend tell map.

quayholt_claims_manager.text: Gordon McLeish is a Claims Manager at Quayholt Insurance.
quayholt_claims_manager.subject: gordon
quayholt_claims_manager.reduceNote: A full staff directory with names and roles hands an attacker a ready-made identity to borrow on a call.

quayholt_claims_head.text: The Claims team reports to the Head of Claims, Ngozi Okonkwo.
quayholt_claims_head.subject: okonkwo
quayholt_claims_head.reduceNote: Publishing the reporting line lets a caller name the right manager, which a weak helpdesk treats as proof of identity.

quayholt_staff_number.text: A conference programme lists Gordon McLeish's Quayholt staff reference as QH-20719.
quayholt_staff_number.subject: gordon
quayholt_staff_number.reduceNote: A staff or employee number is not a secret once it appears in a public document; do not use it as a verification answer.

quayholt_gordon_away.text: Gordon McLeish posted that he is away speaking at an insurance conference this week.
quayholt_gordon_away.subject: gordon
quayholt_gordon_away.reduceNote: A post that puts someone out of the office gives an attacker a believable reason to be calling in a hurry from somewhere new.

quayholt_servicedesk_hours.text: The Quayholt IT service desk opens at 07:00 and resets passwords for staff who are locked out.
quayholt_servicedesk_hours.subject: leila
quayholt_servicedesk_hours.reduceNote: Advertising exactly what the service desk will do, and when, tells an attacker which story to use and when to call before the team is fully awake.

techniques.urgency: Urgency. A rushed reset is the oldest pressure line on a service desk.
techniques.authority_borrowed: Borrowed authority. Naming someone senior does not replace the check.
techniques.deflect: Dodging the checks. A callback on the number on file, or the security questions, is exactly what would catch this, so steering you past it is the tell.

ask.pending: She wants both of her checks before she does it.
ask.refused: She will not reset it on this call.

hints: Find out who the locked-out manager reports to before you call.
The company site names the Head of Claims and lists a staff reference.
Ngozi Okonkwo heads Claims, and Gordon's staff reference is QH-20719 on the events page.

defenderNotes.manager: A helpdesk that calls back on the number already on file does not need to guess whether a manager's name is proof.
defenderNotes.reset_password: Both answers she accepted, the manager's name and the staff reference, were on the public site. A callback to the number on file defeats every line here.

mfaDecision._note: E3 MFA-fatigue beat (11 §3.2), now a learner decision (E3-11). The shell copies this object verbatim into awarenessEpisode.mfa in scenarios/awareness_e3_helpdesk_reset/scenario.json.erb; the runner's `mfa` stage feeds it to the `authenticator` scene via socialOverlayParams. Not scored, and shown only when the pretext call landed (skipMfaIfUnlanded). Decision mode: the learner picks `timing` (when) and `count` (how many), the burst plays (a large count collapses to a '…and N more' summary line, capped at 4 cards), the target taps approve, and the overlay's outcome panel shows the chosen timing's `outcome`, the chosen count's `note` and `defenderNote`. Every combination lands; the text explains which conditions made it work. The old watch-only shape was { pushes[{ at, app, account, location, device }], approvesAt } and is still supported by the scene when `choice` is absent.

choice.intro: You have Gordon's password, but Quayholt still wants a tap on his phone before it lets you in. You send the prompts. Decide when to fire them and how many.

options.label: During working hours
options.outcome: At his desk and alert, Gordon almost reported it. He tapped Approve only because your service-desk call minutes earlier had him half-expecting IT to "sort his sign-in". In daylight, a prompt he didn't ask for is the obvious tell.

options.label: Late evening, off the clock
options.outcome: Half-watching television, Gordon tapped Approve to clear the buzzing without really reading it. Off the clock, people stop treating prompts as work and just swipe them away.

options.label: The early hours
options.outcome: Woken at 02:14, Gordon tapped Approve half-asleep to make his phone stop. Tired and off guard is exactly when a prompt gets waved through.

options.label: Two or three
options.note: A couple of prompts lean on your pretext and the hour more than on wearing him down.

options.label: A dozen
options.note: A steady run of prompts turns it into a nuisance he wants gone, and one tap ends it.

options.label: One after another
options.note: A flood is the loudest version, and the easiest for an alert target, or a rate limit, to catch.

mfaDecision.defenderNote: Gordon's app could stop every version of this. Number matching makes a half-asleep tap useless, a prompt he didn't start is a report and not an Approve, and a rate limit caps the flood.
